# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Critical Reading: The 24-Month Follow-up

This is the most informative document so far. It directly tests the open questions from the earlier papers and settles several of them. But it has its own problems. The most important is one the authors report without connecting it to their decay estimate: two control offices cut their meetings partway through the trial. There is also a calculation, worth doing, that suggests meetings explain more of the gain than the mediation analysis says.

The arithmetic checks out:

- **Varden, timesheet hours:** 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8%.
- **Varden, log hours:** 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5%.
- **Halden subset:** 96.8 / 86.6 = +11.8%, with 34.9 / 40.3 = −13.4% hours.

## 1. What it settles

| Open question from earlier readings | Answer at 24 months |
|---|---|
| Are the per-hour gains entirely an artifact? (Varga and Holm) | **No.** +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8), with record-based output, log-measured hours, randomisation and two years of follow-up. |
| Can novelty be set aside? (meta-analysis) | **No.** The meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, as I suspected. The one controlled long-run study shows some decline. |
| Do timesheets miss work? | Slightly. Log data show hours fell 11%, against 12% on timesheets. |
| Were meeting levels already different before the trial? | **No.** Baselines were similar (7.4 h treated, 7.2 h control). This resolves the concern that month-6 data had no baseline. |
| Did counter waiting times rise relative to control? | **Yes.** 7.3 v 4.0 minutes, now a proper comparison with the control group rather than a treated-only before-and-after figure. |
| Is the model sector-general? | **No.** The county ended the counter arm. All three Halden organisations that reverted cited coverage or client obligations. |

## 2. Control contamination biases the decay estimate

In month 15, two of the seven control offices ran a "meeting audit." Their output per hour then rose by 4.1%. The paper treats this as a side observation about mechanisms. But it also contaminates the control group:

- If two of seven control offices gained about 4%, the control average rose by roughly 1.2 percentage points.
- That shrinks the treatment–control difference at 24 months by about the same amount.
- **So part of the apparent fall from 12.5% to 9.8% may reflect control offices improving, not treated offices fading.**

The meeting audit was very likely prompted by the trial, since treated offices' meeting cuts were visible within the county. That makes it a spillover effect. The intention-to-treat estimate is still valid as a comparison of policies. But it understates the effect of the reduced schedule compared with no change at all, and it overstates decay. The paper should report the 24-month estimate both with and without those two offices.

## 3. The meetings arithmetic suggests an even stronger result than the mediation analysis

Here is a rough calculation using the paper's figures. It assumes meetings count toward timesheet hours.

| | Baseline | 24 months | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treated timesheet hours | 37.9 | ~33.4 (−12%) | |
| Treated meeting hours | 7.4 | 3.9 | −3.5 |
| Treated non-meeting hours | 30.5 | ~29.5 | **about −3%** |
| Output per FTE (relative to control) | | | **−3.4%** |

Control offices' non-meeting time was roughly flat, about +0.7%.

On these numbers, **output per non-meeting hour barely changed.** Treated staff cut almost all of the lost hours out of meetings. They did roughly the same amount of other work as before and produced roughly the same output. If so, nearly the whole timesheet-based per-hour gain comes from removing meeting time, which produced no measurable output, from the denominator. This would leave little room for the 18% attributed to fatigue or the 35% left unexplained.

The two control offices that ran the audit fit the same pattern. They moved about 2.1 hours from meetings into other work, about 7% more non-meeting time, and their output rose 4.1%.

This conflicts with the mediation result, which attributes only 47% of the gain to meetings. The likely source of the conflict is the **definition of log-measured hours**, which the paper doesn't explain:

- If log time counts only time spent working on cases, meetings aren't part of it. In that case, cutting meetings shouldn't raise output per log hour except indirectly, for example through fewer interruptions. And log hours falling 11% would be hard to explain when non-meeting time fell only about 3%.
- If log time includes time logged in during meetings, it is close to presence time and not a "stricter" measure.

The paper needs to state what log time includes. It should also show output per non-meeting hour directly. If my reading is right, the main finding is simpler and more useful than the paper presents: **in this setting, the shorter week worked largely by removing meetings.**

## 4. "Confirms" overstates the mediation test

- **The same offices generated and tested the hypothesis.** The registered test uses the same seven treated offices that produced the exploratory result, with more months added. A pre-specified model guards against choosing a model to fit the data, but it is not an independent replication. "Survives a pre-specified test" is accurate; "confirms" is too strong.
- **The precision seems high for 14 clusters.** A CI of 28–66% on a mediation share across 7 v 7 offices needs a stated inference method, and few-cluster inference was already a concern in the 9-month report.
- **The shares depend on modelling choices.** Fewer meetings probably also reduce fatigue. Splitting the gain into 47 / 18 / 35 assumes the two pathways don't interact and depends on how the model orders them.
- **Confounding is acknowledged but limits the result.** The authors state the assumption of no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome. Meeting cuts were chosen by managers, so offices with more active managers may have cut meetings and improved in other ways too.

## 5. The decay is suggestive, not established

- **The intervals overlap heavily.** At 9 months the timesheet CI was +6.9 to +18.4; at 24 months it is +4.6 to +15.2. The data are consistent with modest fading and also with none.
- **Two time points can't show the trajectory.** The gain may have levelled off or may still be declining. "Declined but not disappeared" is true at month 24 but says nothing about month 36.
- **The summary compares different measures.** It says the gain "fell from 12.5% to 8.5%," comparing a 9-month timesheet figure with a 24-month log figure. That makes the decline look like about a third. The like-for-like decline is about a fifth (12.5 to 9.8), and part of that is contamination (section 2).

The authors are right that the data rule out Varga and Holm's prediction of zero by month 10. Since the 9-month figure was already 12.5%, that was settled before this report.

## 6. Cost is still missing

- **Case-processing offices:** output per FTE is −3.4% at full pay, plus overtime, and this is the third report without a cost per case. Labour cost per case has risen by at least 3.5%, before overtime premiums. It's the figure the county would need.
- **The counter arm's cost estimate looks low.** The paper says restoring service would need 12% more staff and raise cost per contact by 9%. If demand is unchanged, 12% more staff at the same pay serving the same number of contacts implies about +12% cost per contact. The 9% needs explaining: cheaper hires, part-time cover, or some per-hour gain carried through.

## 7. The Halden subset

The authors label it carefully as "survivors twice over" and an upper bound, which is right. Further points:

- **Response bias adds another filter.** 14 of 23 responded, so the sample is filtered three times: completion, continuation and response.
- **The hours baseline may be wrong.** 40.3 is exactly the average across the 27 organisations with time tracking in Varga and Holm's re-analysis. These 11 are a different subset; the 17-organisation subset had 40.4. The authors should confirm the baseline belongs to these 11 organisations.
- **One reversion breaks the two-way classification.** A marketing agency reverted over *client deadlines*. Responsiveness to clients is a kind of coverage obligation inside work usually classed as discretionary. This supports the meta-analysis's warning that the classification is often a mix within one organisation.
- **The original attrition misstatement is not corrected.** R. Okafor co-authored the Halden working paper, which said withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata contradict this. A follow-up co-authored by the original team would be the natural place to correct it, and it doesn't.

## 8. Smaller points

- **Backlogs and deadlines are still not reported.** The 9-month report named backlog build-up beyond statutory deadlines as a risk. Two years later, queue length and deadline compliance are absent. Cases closed per FTE can look fine while the backlog grows or difficult cases are deferred.
- **Resignations are still raw comparisons without CIs** (4.1% v 7.9%).
- **Quality appears stable** (appeal overturn rate 3.2% v 3.0%), but no CI is given.

## Bottom line across all five documents

| Question | Current best answer | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Does output per hour rise? | Yes, about 8–10% in backlog-based work, sustained to 24 months | Moderate, now with randomised long-run support |
| Were the 20%+ headline figures reliable? | No | High |
| Does output per worker hold up? | Nearly in backlog-based work (about −3%); no in coverage-bound work (about −10%, and the counter arm was ended) | Moderate to high |
| Is the model sector-general? | No. Coverage obligations, including obligations to clients, are the dividing line | High |
| Does the gain fade? | Somewhat, possibly less than reported because of control contamination; the trajectory after 24 months is unknown | Low to moderate |
| What drives the gain? | Mostly removing meetings, possibly almost entirely on a simple calculation. Fatigue contributes little or nothing | Moderate |
| Could the gain be had without cutting hours? | Partly, based on two control offices. Untested whether the hours cut is needed to force and sustain the change | Low |
| Does it pay for itself? | Not shown. Cost per unit of output has never been reported, and the available numbers imply it rises | Moderate that it rises |

The practical message is narrower than any single paper's framing. In backlog-based work, a shorter week appears to keep output nearly unchanged, mainly because it forces cuts to low-value meeting time, and it brings real gains in sickness absence and retention. Whether a "meeting audit" alone would capture most of the productivity gain is now the key untested question. A trial arm that reorganises without cutting hours would answer it.
